title: Planetary Information Processing and Memory Storage Through Deep Time: A Bounded Order-of-Magnitude Reconstruction from Prebiotic Chemistry to the Modern Technosphere
plain_title: Counting a planet's memory and computing
thesis: Count everything on Earth that stores or processes information, from the first cells to today's data centers, keep each kind in its own units, and four findings stand out.
summary: The paper builds a census of Earth across 68 moments over 4.10 billion years. At each moment it estimates ten separate quantities: three kinds of DNA storage, two kinds of memory, three kinds of event rate (cell chemistry, nerve signals, chip operations), total power, and how long information persists. Today's values are built bottom-up from published counts of cells, animals and devices across 975 cataloged systems, with uncertainty ranges from 10,000 Monte Carlo draws. Older values are scaled back from those anchors using fossils and rock chemistry.

claims.claim: Life and technology together use a fixed, countable amount of power.
claims.paper_value: 65.0 TW for life plus 19.5 TW for technology, 84.5 TW in all
claims.note: The six compartments in the ledger sum to the stated totals.

claims.claim: Life uses about half of what plants capture from sunlight.
claims.source: Census value for life's power; the 125 TW figure is cited from outside literature
claims.note: The division is right; the 125 TW primary-production anchor comes from published biogeochemistry.

claims.claim: Microbial power and carbon divide cleanly into deep-underground, standby and active surface cells.
claims.paper_value: 77.5 Gt C at 25 fg C per cell (17.25, 48.625 and 11.625 Gt C); 0.69 TW, 3.89 TW and 9.42 TW, totalling 14.00 TW at 10, 150 and 5,000 Hz
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: Section 2.4, Appendix A.1/C.1 and Table B1 all use the uniform 25 fg C per cell and identical per-compartment rates.

claims.claim: The number of microbial cells follows from their total carbon.
claims.paper_value: 3.10×10³⁰ cells from 77.5 billion tonnes of carbon at 25 femtograms per cell
claims.source: Census: microbial carbon divided by carbon per cell

claims.claim: Cell chemistry is the largest event rate on the planet.
claims.paper_value: 2.80×10³³ events a second deterministic central (median 2.70×10³³, 95% range 9.46×10³² to 8.25×10³³)
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: Table MC1 prints both the exact deterministic value and the Monte Carlo median alongside the 95% interval.

claims.claim: All the DNA in living cells can be counted in bits.
claims.paper_value: 3.60×10³⁷ bits in total, 1.84×10³⁷ under selection, 3.80×10¹² unique
claims.note: All three values match the 2026 census row as stated.

claims.claim: Every animal nervous system together fires a countable number of signals.
claims.paper_value: 3.43×10²⁴ neurons, 3.00×10²⁷ synapses, 3.00×10²⁶ signals a second (95% range 9.08×10²⁵ to 9.92×10²⁶)
claims.data_value: 3.43×10²⁴ neurons, 3.00×10²⁷ synapses, 3.00×10²⁶ signals a second (95% range 9.08×10²⁵ to 9.92×10²⁶)
claims.source: Census; synapses × 0.10 signals a second each; uncertainty ledger
claims.note: Text, Table MC1 and Figures 1–3 all plot and cite the exact 95% Monte Carlo range.

claims.claim: Two mass extinctions each removed more than nine tenths of nerve signalling.
claims.paper_value: 94.0% at the end of the Permian (95% range 87.8% to 99.0%), 92.5% at the end-Cretaceous asteroid impact (95% range 84.4% to 98.5%)
claims.source: Census: change between the moments either side of each extinction; uncertainty ledger
claims.note: Both drops recompute exactly from the 68-moment census as constrained paleobiological scenarios.

claims.claim: All the world's chips together execute a countable number of operations.
claims.section: Abstract, finding 3; Table D1; Table MC1
claims.paper_value: 1.89×10²² executed operations a second (95% range 9.31×10²¹ to 3.24×10²²; peak 7.60×10²²), 9.00×10²¹ of them on AI accelerators, drawing 80.0 GW
claims.data_value: 1.89×10²² executed operations a second (95% range 9.31×10²¹ to 3.24×10²²; peak 7.60×10²²), 9.00×10²¹ on AI accelerators, 80.0 GW
claims.note: All four device classes and the updated 95% range match the device and Monte Carlo ledgers.

claims.claim: Chips remain far below nervous systems when everything is added up.
claims.paper_value: 1.59×10⁴ times below all animals (ratio 6.30×10⁻⁵, 95% range 1.57×10⁻⁵ to 2.23×10⁻⁴) and 64.3 times below all 8.1 billion human brains (1.215×10²⁴ synaptic operations per second at 162 GW)
claims.data_value: 1.59×10⁴ times below all animals and 64.3 times below 8.1 billion human brains (162 GW)
claims.source: Census: nerve signals ÷ chip operations; 8.1×10⁹ people × 1.50×10¹⁴ signals each ÷ 1.89×10²²
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: human population is standardised to 8.1 billion across all sections and human brain power to 162 GW (0.162 TW).

claims.claim: One large AI cluster out-runs one human brain in raw operations per second.
claims.paper_value: 3.00×10²⁰ operations against 1.50×10¹⁴ signals a second: 2.0 million times
claims.source: Census: largest single system today ÷ one human brain
claims.note: The division is exact and explicitly contrasts chip operations with synaptic events.

claims.claim: Modern storage holds 15 zettabytes with an 8.30-year unpowered mean lifetime and 9.96×10²³ bit-years of persistence.
claims.paper_value: 1.20×10²³ bits installed; weighted mean unpowered retention 8.30 years (flash 3.5, hard disks 7.0, tape 25); 9.96×10²³ bit-years unpowered; 20.0 GW refresh power (9 GW storage scrubbing + 11 GW DRAM refresh)
claims.data_value: 1.20×10²³ bits, 8.30 years, 9.96×10²³ bit-years and 20.0 GW across both the memory ledger and the 2026 census row
claims.note: Both the memory ledger and the 68-row Table 1 / S1 close identically to 9.96×10²³ bit-years.

claims.claim: The reconstruction spans 68 census moments calibrated on 975 systems, 2,641 measurements, 1,300 sources and 26 parameter anchors.
claims.paper_value: 68 sub-epochs, 975 systems, 2,641 measurements, 1,300 sources, 26 parameter-register anchors
claims.data_value: 68 sub-epochs, 975 systems, 2,641 measurements, 1,300 sources, 26 parameter-register anchors
claims.note: Revised on 24 November 2026: manuscript, appendix and figures include all four newly added evolutionary and historical stops.

rationale.step: Keep ten quantities in their own physical units and never merge them into one composite score.
rationale.note: Bits, events a second, watts and bit-years remain strictly separated across all 68 census moments.

rationale.step: Build today's values bottom-up from published counts and require carbon, cells, devices and power to close.
rationale.note: Every compartment in the text, Table B1, Table D1, Table P1 and the 2026 census row closes identically.

rationale.step: Scale back through deep time from today's anchors using fossils, rock chemistry and living relatives.
rationale.note: There is no direct fossil meter for ancient firing rates, so pre-modern moments remain bounded order-of-magnitude scenarios, as the paper explicitly states.

rationale.step: Compare cell chemistry, nerve signals and chip operations by counting elementary state transitions per second.
rationale.note: Counting transitions per second is physically well defined, though one enzymatic reaction, one synaptic release and one 16-bit multiply are different kinds of work.

rationale.step: Propagate parameter uncertainty across 10,000 Monte Carlo draws.
rationale.note: Deterministic central values, medians and 95% intervals now agree across the abstract, Table MC1 and all figures.

conclusions.conclusion: The world's chips have not overtaken the world's nervous systems in aggregate event rate.
conclusions.note: The joint 95% interval of the chip-to-nerve ratio runs from 1.57×10⁻⁵ to 2.23×10⁻⁴, staying four orders of magnitude below parity.

conclusions.conclusion: One frontier AI cluster exceeds one human brain by two million times in raw operations per second.
conclusions.note: Exact as a raw rate ratio (3.00×10²⁰ ÷ 1.50×10¹⁴), while leaving functional equivalence per operation open.

conclusions.conclusion: Mass extinctions acted as severe bottlenecks that erased over nine tenths of animal nerve signalling before mammal and bird radiations.
conclusions.note: The drops (94.0% and 92.5%) follow cleanly from the paleobiological biomass model, though the ecological release step remains an evolutionary interpretation.

conclusions.conclusion: Modern digital storage holds vastly more bits than ancient archives yet requires 20 GW of continuous power to avoid decay over an 8.3-year unpowered horizon.
conclusions.note: Fully verified across the memory persistence and power closure ledgers.

bottom_line: Following the 9 November and 24 November 2026 revisions, all 68 census moments, 975-system catalog counts, prokaryotic carbon and rate compartments, 8.1-billion human totals (162 GW, 64.3× chip gap), Monte Carlo deterministic centrals and 95% intervals, unpowered storage persistence (9.96×10²³ bit-years) and figures agree across the manuscript, appendix and canonical CSV ledgers. Pre-modern deep-time rows remain bounded order-of-magnitude scenarios rather than direct measurements.
revised: On 9 November 2026, six errors in power units, budget closure, uncertainty intervals, device splits and refresh power were corrected. On 24 November 2026, the manuscript, appendix and figures were expanded to all 68 census moments and 975 cataloged systems, and prokaryotic carbon per cell, the 8.1-billion human baseline, Table MC1 deterministic centrals and the 2026 persistence product (9.96×10²³ bit-years) were unified across every table and ledger.
